result.summary: Juno spots Jupiter hiding mists and asks him for a pretty heifer, which is Io in disguise. He gives her up and Juno sets hundred-eyed Argus to guard her. Io meets her father Inachus and reveals herself by writing in the dust. Jupiter sends Mercury, disguised as a shepherd, to lull Argus to sleep.

scenes.title: Juno claims the heifer
scenes.summary: Juno notices the unnatural mists, finds Jupiter and demands the heifer. Jupiter cannot refuse without raising suspicion, so Juno takes Io and gives her to Argus.
scenes.stakes: Jupiter risks exposing his affair and Juno's wrath; Io risks captivity.

scenes.title: Argus guards Io
scenes.summary: Argus, with a hundred eyes, keeps Io, feeding her by day and tying her at night. She cannot speak or plead and is frightened by her own lowing.
scenes.stakes: Io is imprisoned in animal form, unable to ask for help.

scenes.title: Io and Inachus
scenes.summary: Io visits the banks of her father's river and sees her horns. Unrecognised, she writes her name in the dust, and Inachus laments. Argus then leads her away to distant pastures.
scenes.stakes: Io may never regain her human form or her family; Inachus faces endless grief.

scenes.title: Mercury charms Argus
scenes.summary: Jupiter sends Mercury to kill Argus. Mercury disguises himself as a shepherd, plays pipes and talks, and Argus invites him to sit as sleep tries to take him.
scenes.stakes: Argus's life; Mercury must trick him without being recognised.

alias_notes.explanation: Mercury is called this in the text; in outside tradition his mother Maia was Atlas's daughter, so it is a loose descent title.

notable_quotes.reason: Inachus laments that godhood denies him death's relief from grief.

analysis.text: Divine desire and jealousy cost a mortal her voice and body; Io's inability to speak, then writing in the dust, shows identity persisting through loss.
Ovid draws on older Greek myth of Io and Argus, tying it to the river Inachus and Argive tradition.

legacy.text: Argus Panoptes's hundred eyes gave rise to the English phrase 'Argus-eyed' for a vigilant watcher.

fun_facts.text: The story of Mercury piping Argus to sleep was a popular subject for Renaissance and Baroque painters such as Velázquez and Rubens.

language_notes.text: The braces mark words the translator added for clarity. 'Intrigues of a husband so often detected' means Jupiter's repeated infidelities, which Juno has caught before.
'I am either deceived, or I am injured' means she suspects either she is mistaken or she is being wronged by her husband.
Io is called daughter of Inachus, a river god of Argos. Her father is named instead of her, which is a common epic way to identify a person.
'Daughter of Saturn' is Juno, a child of the Titan Saturn. Jupiter is also his child, so the couple are siblings.
'Sharer of his descent and his couch' means Juno, who is both Jupiter's sister and his wife.
The bracketed number is a translator's footnote marker, not part of Ovid's text. The sense is that the eyes rested in shifts.
Arbute is the strawberry tree, an evergreen shrub whose leaves and fruit were typical rough fodder.
Naiads are nymphs of fresh water. Here they are Io's sisters, daughters of the river-god Inachus.
'A detriment to be a God' means divinity is a burden, because as an immortal river-god Inachus cannot die to escape grief.
Phoroneus was a legendary early king of Argos and son of Inachus. Io is called his granddaughter here, though she is Inachus's daughter, so the wording is loose.
Winged sandals, sleep-bringing wand (caduceus) and cap are Mercury's standard equipment. The cap is the traveller's hat, in other tellings a cap of invisibility.
'Oaten straws joined together' are the pan-pipes, reeds of graded lengths bound side by side, an instrument of Arcadian shepherds.
The pipe's recent invention points to the story of Pan and Syrinx, which Mercury is about to tell Argus.

context_notes.text: Mercury was Jupiter's messenger god, known for trickery and for leading souls. He later lulls Argus to sleep with a tale and kills him.
Argus, the watchman with many eyes, was set to guard Io. His eyes were said to sleep in turns, so he was ever watchful.
Argus, called Panoptes ('all-seeing'), is a giant set by Juno to guard Io, whom Jupiter had turned into a heifer.
Io's hoof-writing is a famous moment: she reveals herself by tracing her name in the dust.
Maia was the eldest of the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas, and the mother of Mercury by Jupiter.
Juno is Jupiter's wife. She is jealous of Io and has made Argus her watchman.

literary_notes.text: The clouds Jupiter makes to hide his deed are what expose it, since unnatural night at midday alerts Juno.
Juno feigns ignorance while knowing the truth, and her questions are a trap that Jupiter must answer with a lie.
Shame and love are set against each other in balanced clauses, showing Jupiter's inner conflict.
Argus's vigilance is exaggerated to the point that even with his back turned he still sees Io, stressing her total captivity.
She wants to stretch out suppliant arms but has none, which makes her transformation cruelly concrete.
The repeated 'knew her not' and 'follows' stress the pathos of a daughter beside her family who cannot recognise her.
Inachus speaks directly to his daughter, and his repeated cry of grief gives the speech pathos.
His hopes of a wedding and grandchildren are overturned in the next sentence, where Io must have a mate from the herd.
'The starry Argus' recalls his many eyes, which resemble stars, and prepares for the story of his death.
Half-sleeping, half-watching, Argus is balanced between rest and vigilance, building suspense before his fall.
